Site effects on detection and false positives

Source: vignettes/site_effects.Rmd
site_effects.Rmd

The automated method rarely detects a species equally well at every occupied site. Recorders placed farther from where animals call, sites with fewer calling individuals, or louder backgrounds lower the chance of a true detection, and covariates in det capture only the part of this that was measured. False positives vary among sites in the same way, with the sources of sound that the classifier confuses with the target. crywolf offers a site random intercept for each process: random_det = TRUE on true detection and random_fp = TRUE on the false-positive rate. They can be used alone or together.

This article describes the two effects, shows in simulations what each one recovers and what it costs, and fits them to the curiango data. The fitting code is shown but not run when the article is built.

The model

In the multiple-methods false-positive occupancy model (Miller et al., 2011), at site i and occasion k of the automated method,

\mathrm{logit}(p_{11,ik}) = \mathbf{z}_{ik}^\top \boldsymbol{\alpha} + d_i, \qquad d_i \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, \sigma_{\mathrm{det}}),

\mathrm{logit}(p_{10,i}) = \gamma_0 + \mathbf{x}_i^\top \boldsymbol{\gamma} + e_i, \qquad e_i \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, \sigma_{\mathrm{fp}}),

where p_{11,ik} is the probability of a detection at an occupied site, p_{10,i} the probability of a false positive at an unoccupied one, \mathbf{z}_{ik} and \mathbf{x}_i the covariates of det and fp, and \gamma_0 = \alpha_1 - \Delta the false-positive intercept, a positive gap \Delta below the detection intercept (vignette("crywolf")). The site effect on true detection, d_i, is reported as sd_det_site (\sigma_{\mathrm{det}}); the one on false positives, e_i, as sd_fp_site (\sigma_{\mathrm{fp}}). Both standard deviations have half-Normal priors with scale 1 (fp_priors(det_site_sd = , fp_site_sd = )). The verified method has no site effect: its detection probability r_{11} is the same at every occupied site, up to the covariates of ver.

The two effects act on different branches of the likelihood. Each site has a single latent state, occupied or not: d_i matters only if the site is occupied and e_i only if it is not. The verified data, which never contain false positives, are what tell the two branches apart.

m <- fp_occu(data, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ 1, random_det = TRUE)
m_both <- fp_occu(data, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ 1, random_det = TRUE, random_fp = TRUE)

With both effects on, fp_occu() warns that the chains mix slowly; the simulations below show why.

Simulations

Design

Each simulated dataset had 300 sites, 20 automated occasions per site, and 30% of the sites verified on 3 occasions each. Occupancy depended on a standardized covariate with intercept 0 (occupancy 0.5 at the mean) and slope -0.8; at the reference, true detection was 0.6, false positives 0.05, and verified detection 0.6. The logit of true detection and of the false-positive rate varied among sites with standard deviations \sigma_{\mathrm{det}} and \sigma_{\mathrm{fp}}, each 0 or 1, which gives four scenarios. Every dataset was fitted with four models: no site effect (base), random_det, random_fp, and both, with the default priors of fp_priors() and 4 chains of 1000 warm-up and 1000 sampling iterations (adapt_delta = 0.95). There were 100 replicates of each scenario, 1600 fits in all, and every model of a replicate saw the same data. The fits used the prototype of the Stan program in dev/random-det/, written before the option entered the package. The package version uses the same likelihood functions and differs only in how it passes a switched-off effect (as a data vector of zeros, which is faster).

The occupancy slope 

ggplot2::ggplot(summ, ggplot2::aes(model, coverage, colour = model)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed") +
  ggplot2::geom_pointrange(ggplot2::aes(ymin = coverage - 2 * coverage_se,
                                        ymax = pmin(1, coverage + 2 * coverage_se))) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ scenario, nrow = 1) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = colours) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Coverage of the slope") +
  panel_theme

Coverage of the 95% interval of the occupancy slope in each scenario. Bars span two Monte Carlo standard errors; the dashed line is the nominal coverage. 

ggplot2::ggplot(summ, ggplot2::aes(model, bias, colour = model)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  ggplot2::geom_pointrange(ggplot2::aes(ymin = bias - 2 * bias_se,
                                        ymax = bias + 2 * bias_se)) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ scenario, nrow = 1) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = colours) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Bias of the slope") +
  panel_theme

Bias of the posterior mean of the occupancy slope (true value -0.8). Bars span two Monte Carlo standard errors.

Coverage stayed between 0.89 and 0.95 in every scenario and model. With 100 replicates, its Monte Carlo standard error is 0.02 to 0.03, so coverage alone separates the models poorly. In the scenario without any site variation all four models gave the same coverage, 0.90, and the same bias, -0.046, away from zero (the slope was estimated slightly steeper than -0.8): a property of this design and its data, shared by every model, not of the site effects. The Monte Carlo standard error of each bias is about 0.016.

The bias is more telling. When true detection varied among sites, the model without site effects attenuated the slope towards zero by 0.050 (detection varying alone) and 0.092 (both varying). random_det removed the first, -0.016, and halved the second, 0.048; with both effects the bias was 0.000. random_fp alone did not help when detection varied: 0.063 and 0.074. When only the false-positive rate varied, no model was clearly biased. The biases are small next to the width of the intervals in this design, which explains why the coverage barely moved.

The standard deviations of the site effects 

sds <- rbind(
  data.frame(sc[c("scenario", "model")], effect = "true detection (sd_det_site)",
             estimate = sc$sd_det_est, truth = sc$sigma_det),
  data.frame(sc[c("scenario", "model")], effect = "false positives (sd_fp_site)",
             estimate = sc$sd_fp_est, truth = sc$sigma_fp))
fits_it <- ifelse(grepl("^true", sds$effect), sds$model %in% c("random_det", "both"),
                  sds$model %in% c("random_fp", "both"))
sds <- sds[fits_it & !is.na(sds$estimate), ]
ggplot2::ggplot(sds, ggplot2::aes(model, estimate, colour = model)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(ggplot2::aes(yintercept = truth), linetype = "dashed") +
  ggplot2::geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.6) +
  ggplot2::facet_grid(effect ~ scenario) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = colours) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Posterior mean of the standard deviation") +
  panel_theme

Posterior means of the standard deviations of the site effects, for the models that estimate each one. Dashed lines are the true values.

random_det recovered the variation in true detection: the median estimate of sd_det_site was 1.03 and 1.08 for a true value of 1. Without such variation it stayed near zero (0.09), where the half-Normal prior keeps the posterior mean slightly above it. Fitted together, the two effects recovered both standard deviations: sd_det_site 1.02 and sd_fp_site 0.98 when both were 1.

random_fp alone did something else. When only detection varied, it estimated a median sd_fp_site of 1.77 although the false-positive rate was the same at every site, and 2.10 when the true value was 1. Variation in true detection makes the number of detections vary among occupied sites more than the model allows, and without a site effect on detection the only place to put that variation is the false-positive rate. The estimates of sd_fp_site are then wrong, and so are the false-positive rates of single sites. A large sd_fp_site alone is therefore not evidence that false positives vary among sites.

Convergence and cost 

conv <- rbind(
  data.frame(summ[c("scenario", "model")], what = "R-hat > 1.01", share = summ$rhat),
  data.frame(summ[c("scenario", "model")], what = "any divergence", share = summ$divergent))
ggplot2::ggplot(conv, ggplot2::aes(model, share, fill = model)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col() +
  ggplot2::facet_grid(what ~ scenario) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = colours) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of fits") +
  panel_theme

Share of fits with a largest R-hat above 1.01 or with any divergent transition.

random_det alone converged in nearly every fit: the largest R-hat exceeded 1.01 in at most 4% of them. random_fp alone mixed poorly whenever detection varied (60% and 40% of fits), the same symptom as its wrong standard deviations. With both effects the share was 7% to 54%, highest when both rates varied. Both standard deviations were recovered, so the two effects appear identifiable in this design, but only through the occupancy state, which is itself uncertain; our reading is that the chains move slowly between explanations of the same detections. Run longer chains with both effects, and check R-hat and the effective sample sizes of sd_det_site and sd_fp_site before using the estimates. Divergent transitions occurred in at most 6% of the fits of any model and scenario.

A fit took about 2 minutes without site effects and 6 to 9 minutes with them, with the four chains run one after another on one core.

Simulation-based calibration

The simulations above use one set of parameter values. Simulation-based calibration checks the model over the whole prior: fp_sbc() draws the parameters from the priors, simulates data, fits the model, and records the rank of each true value among the posterior draws, which should be uniform when the posterior is computed correctly (vignette("calibration")). With the design of the SBC in that article (80 sites, 6 occasions, 200 replicates) and random_det = TRUE:

sim <- simulate_fp(nsite = 80, nocc = 6, seed = 1)
sbc <- fp_sbc(sim$data, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ 1, random_recorder = FALSE,
              random_det = TRUE, reps = 200, parallel = TRUE,
              fit_args = list(chains = 2, parallel_chains = 1, iter_warmup = 400,
                              iter_sampling = 500, threads_per_chain = 1))
summary(sbc)
#> Simulation-based calibration
#>   mean_rank: near 0.5 when the posterior is unbiased; p_uniform: chi-squared
#>   test of uniform ranks (small values flag a problem).
#> 
#>             parameter   n mean_rank p_uniform divergent
#>       det_(Intercept) 200     0.511    0.8165      0.01
#>        fp_(Intercept) 200     0.506    0.3586      0.01
#>                fp_gap 200     0.496    0.7598      0.01
#>       occ_(Intercept) 200     0.488    0.6579      0.01
#>                 occ_x 200     0.491    0.8343      0.01
#>           sd_det_site 200     0.522    0.0882      0.01
#>  verified_(Intercept) 200     0.494    0.8343      0.01
plot(sbc)

Ranks of the true values among 99 posterior draws in 200 replicates of simulation-based calibration with a site effect on true detection (80 sites, 6 occasions). The grey band is the 99% range of each bin’s count under uniform ranks.

No rank distribution departs clearly from uniform; the smallest p-value of the seven tests is 0.088 (sd_det_site), not small once seven are made, and 2 of the 200 fits had divergent transitions. With six occasions per site each d_i is estimated from few detections, so this design tests the hierarchical part of the model under weak information.

The curiango data

The curiango data (Piatti et al., 2026) were fitted in vignette("markov") with and without a term for runs of detections, with the nights at each site as the sites of the model. The run term improved the fit by far, but the posterior predictive check of both models still gave a Bayesian p-value of 0: the number of detections varied among nights more than either model expected. A site effect on true detection is one explanation, since a nightjar calling close to the recorder on one night and farther on another changes the detection probability of the whole night. The four combinations were fitted (dev/precompute-curiango-random-det.R):

fit <- function(markov, random_det) {
  fp_occu(d, occ = ~ temp + rh + moon, det = ~ bio + aci, fp = ~ 1,
          markov = markov, random_det = random_det, random_recorder = TRUE,
          chains = 4, parallel_chains = 4, threads_per_chain = 4, seed = 1)
}
m <- list(independent = fit(NULL, FALSE), markov = fit("time", FALSE),
          random_det = fit(NULL, TRUE), random_det_markov = fit("time", TRUE))

where d is built as in vignette("markov"). The fits with random_det took about 10 minutes each with four chains of four threads, against 5 without it. All four converged: the largest R-hat was at most 1.008, the smallest bulk effective sample size at least 691, with no divergent transitions.

data.frame(model = names(cur$ppc), row.names = NULL,
           ppc_p_value = round(purrr::map_dbl(cur$ppc, "p_value"), 2),
           sd_det_site = purrr::map_chr(names(cur$summary), function(n) {
             if (any(cur$summary[[n]]$variable == "sd_det_site")) ci(n, "sd_det_site") else "-"
           }))
#>               model ppc_p_value         sd_det_site
#> 1       independent        0.00                   -
#> 2            markov        0.00                   -
#> 3        random_det        0.57 1.06 (0.93 to 1.20)
#> 4 random_det_markov        0.46 0.80 (0.69 to 0.92)
cur$loo[c("model", "elpd_diff", "se_diff")]
#>               model elpd_diff  se_diff
#> 1 random_det_markov    0.0000  0.00000
#> 2            markov -112.5801 22.16062
#> 3        random_det -284.2143 37.92443
#> 4       independent -562.0524 64.78959

With the site effect, the posterior predictive check no longer flags the variation among nights: its p-value is 0.57 without the run term and 0.46 with it. This is expected rather than informative: fp_ppc() replicates each night with its own fitted effect, and its discrepancy is computed night by night, so a night effect absorbs what the check measures. Leave-one-site-out comparison, which predicts each night without its own effect, is the better evidence. The estimated standard deviation is large, 0.80 (0.69 to 0.92) on the logit scale with the run term, so the probability of detecting a calling nightjar differs widely among nights. Leave-one-site-out comparison, with the site effects integrated out (no site had a Pareto k above 0.7 in any model), ranks the model with both terms first, ahead of the run term alone by 113 (standard error 22).

The two terms describe different things. The site effect lets whole nights be more or less detectable; the run term makes detections cluster within a night. Only the run term reproduces the observed runs of consecutive detections:

tab <- rbind(observed = as.numeric(cur$runs_observed),
             do.call(rbind, purrr::map(cur$runs_simulated,
                                       function(m) round(colMeans(m)))))
colnames(tab) <- names(cur$runs_observed)
tab
#>                      1   2  3  4 5+
#> observed           760 184 66 33 37
#> independent       1259 146 31  9  4
#> markov             722 182 74 32 34
#> random_det        1142 142 34 12 10
#> random_det_markov  742 173 63 28 37

The occupancy effects of temperature and humidity both move away from zero, by about one posterior standard deviation: with both terms, temperature is -0.33 (-0.50 to -0.17) and relative humidity -0.90 (-1.09 to -0.72), against -0.25 (-0.40 to -0.10) and -0.82 (-0.98 to -0.66) with the run term alone. The intervals overlap broadly; in our reading the ecological conclusions of vignette("markov") do not change.

Leave-one-site-out comparison

loo() compares models by how well each predicts a site left out of the fit. A left-out site has no estimate of its own site effects, so its predictive density averages the likelihood over the distribution of the effects. With random_det or random_fp, loo() computes that integral by Gauss-Hermite quadrature for every posterior draw: 100 nodes with one site effect and a grid of 30 nodes per effect with two (argument nodes). The conditional log-likelihood, with each site’s own effect plugged in (integrate = FALSE), answers a different question and gives many sites with unreliable Pareto k.

Which to use

  • Covariates first. A measured cause of variation in detection (noise, distance, recorder model) belongs in det, and a measured cause of false positives in fp. A covariate costs one coefficient; a site effect costs one parameter per site.
  • random_det = TRUE for variation in true detection among sites that the covariates do not explain. In the simulations it left bias and coverage unchanged when there was no such variation, at about three times the run time, and reduced the bias of the occupancy slope when there was.
  • random_fp = TRUE only together with random_det unless there is reason to think that detection does not vary among sites: alone, it mistakes variation in detection for variation in false positives.
  • Both, when both kinds of variation are plausible, with longer chains and a close look at the diagnostics.
  • None of them fixes false positives that follow an environmental gradient correlated with occupancy. That is a matter for the fp formula (vignette("crywolf")).

References

Miller, D. A., Nichols, J. D., McClintock, B. T., Grant, E. H. C., Bailey, L. L., & Weir, L. A. (2011). Improving occupancy estimation when two types of observational error occur: non-detection and species misidentification. Ecology, 92, 1422–1428. https://doi.org/10.1890/10-1396.1

Piatti, L., de Sousa, D. L. H., Oliveira, B. S., de Melo, A. V., Sugai, L. S. M., & Provete, D. B. (2026). Methodological choices influence ecological inference in passive acoustic monitoring of a Neotropical nightjar. Journal of Avian Biology, in press.
